This topic was also presented at the IV International Conference on HIV Infection in Women and Children in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in collaboration with the Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro and the Institute of Virology of Maryland, USA, in 2002. Garcia MT and colleagues conducted a prospective cohort study in 2005, published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases (Volume 32, Issue 4, Pages 214–219), focusing on the use of PEP following sexual assaults. Similarly, Roland ME et al. explored HIV prevention among sexual assault survivors in Cape Town, South Africa, through an observational study published in AIDS and Behavior in 2012 (Volume 16, Issue 4, Pages 990–998). Wiebe ER et al. shared their 16-month experience offering HIV prophylaxis to sexual assault survivors in a specialized service, as reported in the Canadian Medical Association Journal in 2000 (Volume 162, Issue 5, Pages 641–645). The World Health Organization (WHO) and the International Labour Organization have provided guidelines on PEP to prevent HIV infection, accessible as of April 10, 2013. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) also issued guidelines for PEP in sexually transmitted infections in their 2010 Sexually Transmitted Diseases Treatment Guidelines (Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, Volume 59, Pages 91–93). Jina R et al. contributed to the FIGO Working Group on Sexual Violence/HIV, publishing management guidelines for female survivors of sexual assault in the International Journal of Gynecology and Obstetrics in 2010 (Volume 109, Pages 85–92). In the realm of psychological and mental health interventions, the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (4th edition, 1994) remains a foundational reference. Anderson T et al. systematically reviewed and analyzed psychological treatments for chronic post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in the British Journal of Psychiatry in 2007 (Volume 10, Issue 1, Pages 16–23). Echeburua E et al. examined the treatment of acute PTSD in rape victims through an experimental study published in the Journal of Anxiety Disorders in 1996 (Volume 10, Issue 3, Pages 185–199). Foa EB et al. compared cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and counseling for PTSD in rape victims in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology in 1991 (Volume 59, Issue 5, Pages 715–723). Galovski TE et al. investigated whether CBT for PTSD improves perceived health and sleep impairment in the Journal of Traumatic Stress in 2009 (Volume 22, Issue 3, Pages 197–204). Rahman A et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial in rural Pakistan, demonstrating the effectiveness of CBT-based interventions delivered by community health workers for mothers with depression and their infants, as published in The Lancet in 2008 (Volume 372, Issue 9642, Pages 902–909). Resick PA et al. Rothbaum BO conducted a controlled study on eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) for PTSD in sexual assault victims, published in the Bulletin of the Menninger Clinic in 1997 (Volume 61, Issue 3, Pages 1–18). The WHO has also developed resources such as Psychological First Aid (2011) and guidelines for the pharmacological treatment of mental disorders in primary health care. Additionally, the WHO has issued clinical and policy guidelines for responding to intimate partner violence and sexual violence against women, emphasizing the training of healthcare providers. In terms of healthcare policy and provision, studies have evaluated the effectiveness of training programs for healthcare providers in managing sexual assault and domestic violence cases. For example, Feder G et al. conducted a cluster randomized trial on the Identification and Referral to Improve Safety (IRIS) program for women experiencing domestic violence, published in The Lancet in 2011 (Volume 378, Issue 9805, Pages 1788–1795). Similarly, McLaughlin SA et al. implemented and evaluated a training program for managing sexual assault in emergency departments, as reported in Annals of Emergency Medicine in 2007 (Volume 49, Issue 4, Pages 489–494). Mandatory reporting of intimate partner violence has also been a topic of research. Feldhaus KM et al. examined physicians' knowledge and attitudes toward mandatory reporting laws in Annals of Emergency Medicine in 2003 (Volume 41, Issue 1, Page 159). Sachs C et al. evaluated the impact of mandatory reporting laws on medical facility referrals to police, as published in Annals of Emergency Medicine in 1998 (Volume 31, Pages 488–494). The WHO and other organizations continue to emphasize the importance of monitoring and evaluating the implementation of guidelines and training programs to improve the healthcare response to sexual violence and intimate partner violence.
